description: Situation-first decision reviews that connect a real decision to reviewed cognitive-bias lenses, decision skills and practical techniques.

situations.title: Hiring and interviews
situations.summary: Review candidate judgments before confidence, first impressions or outcome stories become stronger than the evidence.
signals: One early impression is shaping the rest of the interview.
The team is using different criteria for different candidates.
A previous hire's success or failure is dominating the next decision.
questions: What criteria were fixed before meeting the candidate?
Which evidence would change the current ranking?
Would the same evidence be judged the same way for another candidate?

situations.title: Project estimation
situations.summary: Estimate time and effort with an outside view instead of relying only on the current plan.
signals: The estimate starts from one target date.
Comparable completed work is not being used.
The plan assumes dependencies will behave normally.
questions: What happened in comparable completed work?
What range is supported by the reference class?
Which assumptions would move the estimate toward either end?

situations.title: Production incident review
situations.summary: Separate what was knowable during an incident from what became obvious only after the outcome.
signals: The cause now feels obvious.
A single recent incident is driving a broad process change.
People are judging the decision mainly by the outcome.
questions: What was actually known at each decision point?
Which alternative explanations were plausible then?
What process change is supported by repeated evidence rather than one vivid event?

situations.title: Product prioritization
situations.summary: Review roadmap choices without letting the loudest request, recent event or prior investment define value.
signals: One customer story dominates the discussion.
A feature stays high priority because much work is already invested.
Success criteria are being added after the preferred option is chosen.
questions: What outcome are we optimizing before comparing features?
Would we fund the next step if no work had already been spent?
What broader evidence competes with the vivid request?

situations.title: Vendor or tool selection
situations.summary: Compare tools using precommitted criteria rather than demos, authority or the first price shown.
signals: A polished demo is being treated as proof of fit.
The first commercial number frames later negotiation.
The preferred vendor is receiving easier questions than alternatives.
questions: Which capabilities must be demonstrated in our environment?
What would we value before seeing the vendor's first number?
What evidence would make us reject the current favourite?

situations.title: Forecasting under uncertainty
situations.summary: Make a forecast that can later be checked, updated and learned from.
signals: A forecast is expressed as one precise number.
The latest event dominates the probability estimate.
Assumptions are not recorded before the outcome.
questions: What reference class is available?
What range is more defensible than one point estimate?
What new evidence should trigger an update?

situations.title: Performance review
situations.summary: Judge performance without letting one recent result or known outcome rewrite the quality of the underlying work.
signals: The latest success or failure dominates the review.
A good outcome is being used as proof that the process was good.
Examples are chosen after the overall rating is already preferred.
questions: What evidence covers the full review period?
How good was the process before the outcome was known?
What evidence would support a different rating?

situations.title: Negotiation
situations.summary: Protect a negotiation from the first number and from pressure to justify a position already taken.
signals: The first offer is setting the range.
The team cannot explain its independent reservation point.
New evidence is being used only to defend the public position.
questions: What is our independent estimate before the anchor?
What evidence changes our reservation point?
Which alternative package would meet the same underlying interests?

situations.title: AI-assisted research
situations.summary: Use AI to expand research without treating fluent text, repeated output or model confidence as verification.
signals: The model's first answer becomes the research frame.
Important claims have no inspectable source.
Several generated summaries are counted as independent confirmation.
questions: What did we believe before asking the model?
Which claims are verified outside the model?
How many genuinely independent sources support the conclusion?

situations.title: Checking a repeated claim
situations.summary: Test whether repetition represents independent evidence or only makes a claim feel familiar.
signals: The same claim appears across many summaries.
Sources point back to one origin.
A correction exists but the old explanation still drives reasoning.
questions: What is the earliest reliable source?
How many independent sources actually exist?
What supported explanation should replace the corrected claim?

situations.title: Career change
situations.summary: Compare staying, moving or reskilling without letting salary anchors, sunk time or today's mood decide the future.
signals: The first salary number dominates the comparison.
Years already invested are treated as a reason to keep investing.
Current frustration is being projected far into the future.
questions: What criteria matter before comparing offers?
Would the next year still be attractive if the past investment disappeared?
What small reversible test could reduce uncertainty?

situations.title: KPI and benchmark review
situations.summary: Check whether a score is still a useful proxy for the real goal and whether the comparison is being interpreted consistently.
signals: Improving the metric is discussed as if it automatically improves the goal.
A single benchmark number hides different operating conditions.
A good score is being used to defend the process without checking consequences.
questions: What real outcome is this metric supposed to represent?
What important behaviour can improve the score without improving the goal?
Would we make the same decision if the score were hidden and only underlying evidence remained?
